utterances.text: I take it you are not the only official in that party. Is there a board and are you the president of that board?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The party has its Assembly or congress, and then it has its general council, which has 60 members, and it has its Presidency. I was and remain a member of the Assembly, of the general council, and of the Presidency of my party. And these elections are held every four years. Now they're held every two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suppose, Dr. Rugova, that other parties, political parties, that is, in Kosovo are organised in a comparable way, having a council or a board and a president?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The other parties are organised by law in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1998/1999, were there contacts between the non-Serb parties in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had contacts, and we operated as political parties, as Albanian political parties, such as the Christian Democratic Party, the Liberal Party, the Social Democratic Party, the Parliamentary Party and others, and we had contacts with other parties; Bosnian parties, Turkish parties, which existed at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there regular communications, meetings, or other forms of exchange of information between the councils or boards of these parties?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was, as need arose and according to people's requirements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these regular communications or meetings?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took the form of meetings, joint meetings, exchange of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the KLA take a part in these contacts?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the KLA did not take part in these political councils. It had its own political parties, I think, in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which political party represented the political ideas of the KLA in those days, 1998/1999?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't have a party, but it had a political representative, it seems to me. It had a representative that spoke for the KLA. I believe it was Mr. Demaci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this representative take a part in these regular meetings and contacts between the political parties?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not take part. But he did this job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he attend these kind of meetings?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did members of your council or board communicate with members of the council or board of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had contacts in the fields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. In your evidence, you indicated that there were some unofficial contacts with the KLA, local people, because many of your members in the districts had joined the armed movement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had contacts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they contacts on the level of the council or board of your party and those of the council or board of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no contacts at the level of the councils.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any information obtained by people on the ground level, so to say, brought upwards to your board, related to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. I said there were contacts, and we received information through the media and other forms of contact that existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was, Dr. Rugova, whether any information related to the KLA obtained by members in the district brought upwards to your board.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information was received at the district level and at the grassroots, and it came to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a system or was it by incident?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Contacts were intermittent because it was difficult to communicate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you assist the Court in explaining what your sources of information were in 1998/1999 to keep you updated of what was going on in Kosovo in these years?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the Kosova Information Centre, which reported on the situation in Kosova on a continuous basis. There were some newspapers which appeared. Now and again there was a satellite television programme which was broadcast from Albania, as I have said in my evidence, from where we could have access to European, American, world media outlets. It was a whole system of information that we had set up in our parallel system in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Kosovo Information Centre, was that organised by the LDK or by all political parties or even more interested parties?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was organised by LDK as well as by the government of Kosova, but it represented the independent opinions of all the political parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you consider yourself as well-informed in 1998/1999, Dr. Rugova?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the existing conditions, I would say yes, I was well-informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about the actions of the KLA in these two years?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The activity of the KLA was reported through information media about the clashes between the Belgrade police and the army and the KLA and the consequences of it. We could all see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this anterior or posterior information?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly posterior, because it was difficult, you know, to communicate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Finally, I've got a few questions about the Serbian government and the accused. It appears from your evidence that you met with the accused only three times in 1998 and in 1999; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1998. On the 15th of May, as I have testified in my evidence, then during the wartime, as I say in my evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In 1999 twice; April the 1st and May the 4th.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also in May, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During the last two meetings, NATO was bombing and you had openly welcomed the NATO attacks. Were you afraid during these two meetings with the accused?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I welcomed the NATO bombing. I was also afraid. I had to be cautious in what I did in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking then that you could not speak openly or in a detailed way about your concerns about the way the Serb forces acted against the Kosovo population during the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your third meeting was only concerned with your wish to travel with your family to Italy because Kosovo, as you said, was empty; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes, that's right. That was the main focus of our talk, that is, for me to leave Kosova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No other relevant issues were touched on?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Rugova, in your evidence, you referred to what you described as Belgrade did this or decided so-and-so. What do you know about the decision-making in Belgrade? Now, I'm not asking you to pass hearsay evidence.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know much because I was not part of those circles or part of the system, but we know who was in leadership then in Belgrade. We know from the accused to the others who were in office then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Finally then, Dr. Rugova, what do you factually know yourself about the alleged role of the accused in relation to deportations or killings or rape or plunder and persecution? What do you know yourself on a factual basis?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a factual basis, I know what I saw, what occurred. The accused had the office that he had. That we know of. He was the President and the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces and of the police forces. I don't need to make any further comments on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's all I ask, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One or two matters do arise, Your Honours. First of all, constitutional issues. As the Court may expect, I plan to call a constitutional expert in due course, and it may be Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 4359 to 4367. constitutional matters of detail are best put off until then, but I am in a position, in case either or any of the Court wish to consider them, to provide the relevant constitutions both in English and in Serbian now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, can we deal with that? They're quite bulky. There's the federal republic's constitution, and there's also the Serbian republic's constitution, which was referred to by the accused, particularly this morning when he was dealing with its Article 6. So if we can make those available. They can be given appropriate exhibit numbers. But I shan't necessarily ask this witness any questions about it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Constitution will be Prosecutor's Exhibit number 131.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, Your Honour, I'd like to say a few words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just let us deal with these procedural matters first, and then of course you can add something. Once we've got everything.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay. And the Serbian Constitution, Your Honours, will be Exhibit -- Prosecutor's Exhibit number 132.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the dates of these two?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the dates are on one of them but not on the other. The Serbian document, as you'll see on the second page, is copyrighted in 1994, but on the third page, Introductory Notes, Constitution of the Republic of Serbia, 28th of September, 1990. If Your Honours would be good enough to go to the other document, which is the federal constitution, but flick through towards the first page or thereabouts of the Cyrillic version which accompanies it. You'll see, in Cyrillic, the 21st of February, 1974, at the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While we're dealing with that, it may be sensible to deal with the poster.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you still have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I haven't got the poster back yet because I handed it back to the Registrar, and I haven't received a copy back, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does the registry have it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've requested copies to be made. They're on their way. And we will submit them as Defence Exhibit number 1, but we will not admit them until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we need to think about that for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, before I turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Rugova wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that if you could take into consideration the constitution of Kosova of 1990 and of 1974. That is by the constitution of the former Socialist Federation of Yugoslavia, because at that time, Kosova had its own constitution. That is all I wanted to say. Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have one question, really, about constitutional matters, perhaps divided into a couple of parts, arising from the cross-examination, and they are these:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Rugova, do you yourself have any legal training? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You think by profession? I am a literary critic and scholar, but I've never had any legal training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've been asked several questions by Mr. Wladimiroff about constitutional matters and about the parallel institutions. Just help us with this, please: So far as you were aware, was the suspension of Kosovo's autonomy lawful or unlawful when it occurred?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was unlawful. Under the constitution of the former federation, that is former Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, it was unlawful, also under the constitution of Kosova, as well as under the then-Constitution of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And of course, you told the Judges last week about the way in which the law was passed in Kosovo with the tanks and so on. Following that which you regarded as an unlawful withdrawal of your autonomy, did you regard there as being any lawful government operating from Serbia that had a right to control Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following the withdrawal of the autonomy and the Kosova constitution, then Serbia - Belgrade - decided to establish its own government in Kosova, which was described as a representative responsible for Kosova. I don't know how to say. A governor, sort of governor from Serbia. We didn't have any government per se. This is how it operated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, a little bit more -- or perhaps I'll just deal with the Exhibit D1 that it's to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The pamphlet that was shown you and that you summarised for us and that the accused read to you, was that a pamphlet you'd ever seen before?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I hadn't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a pamphlet or were -- had you ever seen any similar pamphlets to that before?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a copy of it put or thrown in front of my home like they did with many others, but I was not familiar with the text. I had never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were they throwing this type of pamphlet at your house?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly when they did that, but I think it was prior to 31st of March, or close by that date. I don't know who did that. It was very difficult for someone to distribute such leaflets. I don't know who could have done that. Maybe a group of policemen or some other groups. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that you recall having similar leaflet or leaflets thrown at your house, was it practically possible for Kosovo Albanians to be distributing such leaflets?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very hard indeed to distribute such leaflets all over the city, because it was very difficult to circulate and to move around, especially at night. It was very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time of their distribution, who did have access to the part of the city?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such leaflets have been distributed to several parts of the city. Those who could circulate freely were only the military, the police, other paramilitary groups, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that the leaflet has come back, Your Honour, and very helpfully has been copied in the red colour as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we pass from it, Dr. Rugova, would you like to have it and read it to yourself. I don't need you to read it out loud, but take your time to read it, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you wish me to read it out loud or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, to yourself. And I wish you to read it and see if there's anything in the text that helps you one way or the other to identify who might be its author or who might have been responsible for it. But take your time, as you haven't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to say who the author might have been but I see some linguistic mistakes we don't make in Albanian here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point them to us just so that -- tell us, first of all, which line they're on or -- and then read out the passage.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are more spelling mistakes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we have it on the ELMO, and perhaps the witness can point to the mistakes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Rugova, if you could put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He's highlighting the passages at the moment. Perhaps the marked version in due course can become a sub-part of the exhibit itself, except that it then acquires a Defence Exhibit number. Perhaps it can be D1A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It can be D1A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Rugova, you have highlighted several passages. Are they spelling or grammatical errors, can you help us, please?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are more spelling, orthographical mistakes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you point to the version on the overhead projector. The usher will assist.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First line. You see here the title, you see, "Compatriots," an "E" with two dots is missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then the first line, they were temporarily "perkohesisht," in Albanian it needs a schwa, which is the same letter, "E" with two dots. The second paragraph also -- sorry, the third paragraph, first line. This word, "settling of accounts," "hesapeve," the word in Albanian, also doesn't need an "E" with two dots, schwa that is. And the words "in a position," it doesn't need a schwa. These are some spelling mistakes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And "ovakuohen" you've also mentioned. Further down, at the bottom. Right. Did you have anything whatsoever to do with this document or any document like it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I had nothing to do with it or any such documents. I have not issued it. I have not seen it. Someone may have written it, someone who doesn't have a very good mastery of the Albanian, but not myself. And I have not seen it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Rugova, you were asked a couple of questions by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, may I just ask? Dr. Rugova, you told Mr. Nice that you saw a copy of a similar document which was thrown near your home, your house. Did you actually pick up the document and read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said I haven't seen this document, and I haven't drafted it. But someone has brought it to me after he found it near my house, after they had distributed, a copy, similar copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And did you then read it when it was brought to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I read it, as well as many citizens who were concerned over it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you do anything in relation to it? Did you take any action in relation to it? It's a document that purports to have been issued by you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was unable to take any actions whatsoever. Someone may have written it and put my name underneath, but I couldn't do anything about it. As well as the logo, the KLA, on top of it. If I had issued it, I would have used my own insignia, my own logo. I have my own logo as the President of the Republic of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps one last question about this document, Dr. Rugova. By the time you saw it or something similar to it, you think it was the 30th of March. So the bombing was well under way, but can you, from your knowledge of your compatriots, calculate what might have been the effect of such a document on Kosovo Albanians at that time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this happened before 31st of March. And I don't think it may have had a very large impact on the population, even though it has concerned them and warned them. I explained the reasons on Friday for the expulsion of the population. But I believe it has created some problems. It has worried some people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. One other question arising from the questions of Mr. Wladimiroff. You were asked about your direct knowledge of the accused. You were asked about his responsibility or your knowledge of his responsibility, and you gave an answer explaining what his position was. When you challenged him at that first meeting or on any subsequent meeting, was any other figure identified as bearing responsibility for what was being done by Serb forces in Kosovo, apart from the accused?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the figures are concerned, I said that we don't have yet complete figures. About 10.000 killed, and 4.000 missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My mistake for not making the question clear. Mr. Wladimiroff asked you about the responsibility or your knowledge of the responsibility of the accused. Was anybody else ever identified as bearing responsibility for the --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The accused knew of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I won't take that any further. Now, there's one document I'd like you to look at. It's been -- well, a couple documents, or one in particular. This has been referred to by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court will remember -- the Court will remember that the accused asked the witness about a document that the accused said was numbered 030666. That's the B/C/S translation of what was an English original, so I think it would be helpful if we look at the English original on the ELMO and produce that in part. It's a long interview, but in order that I can get the witness to deal with the accused's questions, there are just two passages we should look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is an interview purported to be given by the accused; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it's only in English, Dr. Rugova, but we'll get its setting first. If we look at the top of the first page, it describes how you, the President of the Republic of Kosovo, on the Kosovo elections, the Serbian regime and opposition, union with Albania, and the southern front -- I hope the interpreters have got these in their booths -- it goes on to say: "The Human Rights Foundation of the United States Congress awarded its highest honour this year to Albanian democracy. In October, it will be received by Dr. Ibrahim Rugova, President of the Republic of Kosovo, and Sali Berisha, President of Albania. To date, the award has been received by Vaclav Havel, the Dalai Lama, and the Chinese Student Movement." Now, do you remember this interview, Dr. Rugova?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the award, but I wasn't asked for any interview. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "In the former premises of the Kosovo Writers Society where the Democratic Alliance of Kosovo is now temporarily residing, Ibrahim Rugova, after all the predicted newspaper delegations had taken turns visiting him, showed me a fax that had arrived for the President of the Republic of Kosovo, that is for him, from Washington. He added that at this time, the award was very important to Albanians and that the Albanian name was now entering Europe and the world after the complete isolation in which Albania had lived and in spite of the repression that was still a reality in Kosovo." And then we have the interviewer, whose name appears to be Lebar. Do you remember the interview?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the interview, but I can find that out and let you know. I remember the award. I mean, I was informed of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But not the interview. I don't remember. Maybe someone has asked me about the award, but I don't remember to have given any special interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just read now about four answers, two on this page and one on the following and then ask for your comments about the answers. Lebar is reported as asking: "Can we also interpret the award that you recently received as international approval of the idea of uniting Kosovo and Albania?" And this, I think, is what the accused was asking you about. You're said to have replied: "Of course we're also counting on that, but our desire is primarily to promote ourselves as the Albanian people, to strengthen political integration and to enter Europe. The border that has separated us from Albania has so far been too much like the Berlin Wall." You were asked: "How unnatural is the border with Albania?" You said: "It is completely unnatural. It is a border that has separated Albanians. We often say of Albania that it is the only state that borders on the territory of its own people." And then it says -- or Lebar goes on to deal with predictions that Serbia and Albania will partition Kosovo. If we go to the second sheet, please, in the middle of the page, we see Lebar, the interviewer, apparently asking you: "Is Kosovo's existence within the borders of Serbia in a confederation still likely?" To which you reply: "That has not been in our programmes for a long time. We want an independent, open Republic of Kosovo as a neutral state between Serbia and Albania. That would be the best solution for a certain period. The purpose of the elections was also to gain legitimate representatives for Kosovo which will be a small state like all the states that arose from the former Yugoslavia republics." Now, I don't want to take time going through all of the interview. There may be other passages of interest. But do the answers that I've read out fit with your opinions being expressed at that time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. This paragraph is more an accurate reflection of my official view, that we wanted an independent Kosova as a neutral state between Serbia and Albania; but in the other section, there are elements that coincide with my views but it might have been taken by journalists and put together somehow. And this text has been -- this text has been put together by the compiler and called an interview. And I would have to verify it. Of course I talked about the Albanians and the border, and in this paragraph, that is my official position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be helpful if this document is given an exhibit number since the accused wanted to rely on it. Probably it should technically be a Defence exhibit but I'm entirely relaxed about it being a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would be easier if it's a Prosecution exhibit since you produced it. Can you tell us where it's from and a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't at the moment. We've managed to dig this much up about it for the time being. The date we don't know. The witness may be able to tell us what year he received this award.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, Dr. Rugova?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No doubt it was 1993 or 1994, but I will tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you say tell us about it. Tell us about the document or the award?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And -- both the award and the document. I'll look into it. It could be from sometime between 1993 and 1995. I remember I received it rather earlier than -- rather early.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if there's further information, I'll bring it to the Court's attention.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 133.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On a similar topic, or broadly similar topic, the Court will recall, when examining Dr. Rugova in chief, we spoke of a declaration in October 1991. It's paragraph 10 of the summary. We did not have at that stage any version available of the position stated by the witness. We now do have a document, one's come to hand, only in English. It sets out the three options spoken of by the witness in his evidence and, to some degree, tracks the attitude of the interviewee in the interview we've just been looking at. Might this be produced, for completeness? I think it would probably be helpful. It's a one-and-a-half-page document in English, and I will try and find a version in another language if one exists. The extract is from the original produced, which is an LDK pamphlet. So may that be the exhibit and the extracts we've got be exactly that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's of the LDK.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 134.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if this can go on the ELMO. We don't need to look at all of it because it's available for review later but we see at the bottom - and this will remind the Chamber of the evidence you gave - dated the 12th of October, 1991. Second to last paragraph on that page: "Albanian political parties in Yugoslavia, being determined to pursue a peaceful and democratic solution of all questions on the basis of the right of people to self-determination according to the principles of CSCE and the conference of Paris, offer the following options for the solution of the Albanian question in Yugoslavia as well as the Yugoslav crisis in general." And the next paragraph reminds us of what you said in answer to me last week. "If the external and internal borders of Yugoslavia remain unchanged, then Kosova must have the status of a republic as a sovereign and independent state with the right of joining an alliance of other sovereign states in Yugoslavia." And the top paragraph sets out population composition and ends with: "As to the question of the Serbs, the Montenegrins, and other ethnic groups in Kosovo, we naturally guarantee all national and civil rights." Then: "Albanians in Macedonia, accounting for 40 per cent of the population, as well as in Serbia and Montenegro, should have the status of a state-forming element and should enjoy all national and civil rights." Then the document goes on to another possibility: "If internal borders between the republics are to be changed, demand of the Albanians in Yugoslavia as an Albanian republic in Yugoslavia on the basis of ethnic and other principles that apply for the Serbs, the Croats, the Slovenes, and other peoples of Yugoslavia." And then the third alternative: "If the external borders of Yugoslavia are to be changed, the Albanians in Yugoslavia request that decisions about reunification of Kosovo and other Albanian territories in Yugoslavia with Albania are made through a plebiscite under international monitoring." And then it goes on to set out some certain matters of history, with your name, and identifies the political parties present at the time. Any other comments about this beyond what you gave us last week when giving evidence, Dr. Rugova?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no further comment. This was -- this is a document that was approved by the Albanian political parties of Kosova, Macedonia, Southern Serbia, and Montenegro, and I have no other specific comment beyond what I said the other day. This is a valid document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The accused, in the course of cross-examination of the witness, I think raised concerns about the absence of a Serbian version of the Rambouillet agreement. We certainly have that available if he wants it, if the amici want it. I don't know whether the Chamber wants it or not but it's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let it be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While that's happening and to save time, the Court will remember that we took versions of that agreement in English and of the education agreement from a book. That's the "Kosovo Conflict," which I'm holding up, which is Kosovo Conflict, a diplomatic history through documents." We've only, I think, got the one version. I hope we may retain it with copies being sufficient for the Chamber's purpose, but I can provide one further document about the education agreement in a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, Dr. Rugova referred earlier to the Kosovo constitutions, two constitutions. I think it would be useful for us to have copies of those as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Microphone, please. We can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I also send a copy of the constitution of the Republic of Kosova, which I have with me, and also a copy of the constitution of 1974. I will send them to you. I have them here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They will be copied and made available to the Chamber tomorrow, I hope, at the latest. But may we just look at one other document in relation to the education agreement. It's an original with a part translation. Your Honour, it has -- it hasn't been possible to find a full version of the agreement in the Serbian and this may be because it simply was never published in full in the Official Gazette. We may be able to obtain one from somewhere else but not the Official Gazette. And the agreement was touched upon, so far as our research has revealed, to a very limited extent in a document coming to the witness and the accused and the amici now. And the translation is a part only of the Official Gazette. And if the original could be placed on the overhead projector. On, I think, the left-hand side, at the bottom, 933. The original on -- yes, on the left-hand side. No. The original, please. On the left-hand side, 933, so that it may be viewed. Further down. Now that, in translation, if we can place the English translation on the ELMO, is an extract the Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia, 12th of September, 1996, and it reflects the education agreement in this way: "Pursuant to Article 29 of the law on the government of the Republic of Serbia, the government of the Republic of Serbia has made a decision," and then it sets out: "The following persons are appointed as members into the group for implementation of the agreement on the return of Albanian students and teachers to schools in the Autonomous Region of Kosovo and Metohija." And then under II, it says: "This decision is to be published in the Gazette."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Rugova, do you know one way or another whether the full text of the education agreement was ever published in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was published in the official Gazette of Serbia or not. You see the names of the working group. But we published in all the media in Kosova at that time. I didn't receive this Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a few other questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: May we have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Since this is an excerpt, we'll go -- we'll exhibit it as Prosecutor's Exhibit 127A ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't been able to locate original versions of any of the newspaper articles cross-examined on by the accused. I've managed to extract part of the article by David Binder or Binder of November 1987, and there's only one line from that that I would like the witness's comment on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember being asked questions -- and I've got the extract available for the Court if it wants it but it may decide it doesn't. You were asked questions about an article said to have been written by David Binder. Do you know him as a journalist or what his interests were?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know David Binder. I know him. He often wrote about Kosova. He wrote some good articles and some others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his standpoint or interest, if he had one that was identifiable?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I had contacts with him, he was very concerned about the situation in Kosova, and he wrote about the violence and the things that happened to the Albanians. And I remember a case in 1990 when there were demonstrations in Kosovo when about 50 people were killed and he went to visit a family near Prishtina where a young girl of 15 had been killed, Fatime Humoli [phoen], and he was very upset. Yes, I know Binder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the extracts that were being put to you by the accused, I think from the version I have, were being -- were accounts of what other people were saying rather than perhaps his own account. In his own account, he's reported as saying this, and I'd like your comment on it: "For the moment, Mr. Milosevic and his supporters appear to be staking their careers on a strategy of confrontation with the Kosovo ethnic Albanians." Would that be a view about which you would like to comment? Accept it, reject it, or comment on it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no comment. That's how it was. That's how it is. His remark was in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the more we have these opinions of various journalists, the less value they are to the Chamber. These are -- I'm not criticising you for re-examining on it since there was cross-examination. These are the opinions of people who happened to go there at the time and writing on it for newspapers. Evidence comes in the form of evidence which is put before the Trial Chamber. If they want to give evidence, of course they can, and that will be listened to. We've allowed the witness -- the accused, rather, to cross-examine the witness upon them, but it must be understood that the only evidence is that which the witness gives. If the witness agrees with some comment, then of course it does become evidence, but otherwise, it's pure comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm heartened to hear that. Our concern has, of course, always been that these things are frequently taken out of context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, if there is examination on it, of course you're entitled to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A couple of questions arising from the accused's questioning this morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked a number of things about the arrangements made for you to go to Italy. I noticed it wasn't challenged that it was first suggested to you you should leave your family behind you. Your preference would have been not to have gone to Italy but to have gone to Macedonia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked to go to Macedonia, which was closer, but I decided -- the accused decided that I should go to Italy. He was able to decide about these things at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in my testimony, I didn't agree to go without my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, had you gone to Macedonia, would there have been Kosovo Albanians there loyal to you and to whom you would have had loyalty? Were there any such Albanians or many such Kosovo Albanians in Italy?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Macedonia, I wouldn't have had any problems with the Albanians. I paid a visit on the 19th of May, 1999. I visited the refugee camp at Stankovac. Whereas in Italy, there are Albanians. There are local Albanians. There are Albanians in Rome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, or I think finally -- second to last. You were asked about Sinan Hasani and his role in events, and you spoke of this, the federal parliament's response. You said, "Everything was provided for." Can you explain what you meant by the phrase "everything was provided for" when speaking about the man Hasani?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, he was -- this is 1987 or 1988. On the basis of the system of the former federation, every federal entity, according to rotation, had its turn. And it came to his turn, and he held the leadership for one year. We also had deputy presidents of the former federation because it was a rotation system of the communist leadership. And there was Fadil Hoxha, Mahmut Bakalli was there --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. It may be that what the accused was suggesting was that he was in some way involved in a way that showed approval of constitutional changes. If that's what was being suggested, what would your comment be?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, he -- he got mixed up, I would say in a negative way. He agreed. He was implicated, I would say. That's how I remember it. But the former federal parliament should have decided this kind of issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, you were asked in the most general way about the possibility of the United States and you being in an agreement that involved both the exodus of people from Kosovo and linked that to the early entry of troops. Was there any such agreement made by you and any American whereby the exodus of people from Kosovo was going to be linked with the incoming NATO or American troops?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM RUGOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Please. This is a fabrication. This is untrue. This is, I would say, a lie. There was never any case of this kind. It was never discussed at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Rugova, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. We're adjourned now. We will sit again in 20 minutes. No. No more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One on each side. Just a moment. Are you going to be fairly quick?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very quick. I think very quick, but -- fairly quick. The 1990 Kosovo constitution we have, it will be copied, distributed. May the same number be retained for any earlier constitution when it's provided by Dr. Rugova, if there is 1974 constitution. Second point is this: Back to the question of location binders, and the Court will remember that the amici are being asked to and have agreed to use the binders served on them and simply to extract the irrelevant material. There are 36 such binders altogether. The accused now has the assistance of lawyers who respect the Court and who are under terms of, no doubt, cooperation with the Court. All this material, 36 binders, has been served on the accused, and I've waited a time, but those representing him must now be in a position to assist with sorting the material, and we simply cannot go on on the basis of copying everything twice for the assistance of the accused because he doesn't or doesn't choose to go to that room. Now, I would invite the Court so to express itself as to encourage, or indeed even compel, the lawyers to make themselves available for sensible contacts with me and those in my teams on matters that will assist the good management of this case, and in the short run to sort out and make available for the accused to use in court the relevant binders, because frankly, to have to copy another 36 binders is extremely wasteful, very time-consuming and something we shouldn't be engaged in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll think about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And on a slightly related topic, I'm asked, sensibly ahead of the time when the problem arises, to inquire of you this: Laws, typically - laws of any country - don't need to be produced as exhibits because they can simply be referred to. They exist. In this case, we could try and forecast all the relevant laws that we may need to refer to and then try and produce them as part of our compendious production of matters to be admitted. Or the Chamber could say, Well, a law is a law. When you need to refer to the law of the former Yugoslavia, it's there and you can refer to it. It would assist us to know, at some stage, whether you want all the laws to be gathered up, we hope comprehensively, but it will probably be quite an exercise, or whether laws can be simply dealt with as matters to which reference may be made as and when necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The only difficulty is we will need access to them in one form or another, and if you've got a copy of the laws, so much the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But we can always produce them when it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Or you can produce them in a comprehensive way, if they're in a volume or something of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we can think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, the translated version of the Rambouillet agreement will be Exhibit number 128 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, something to do with what Mr. Nice said a moment ago and then I'll go on with the questions that I wanted. First of all, nobody represents me. The fact that I am allowed to communicate with my two advisors, associates, does not mean that they are my representatives. They are my associates. Therefore, I consider that the circulation of material should be enabled as is suited to me. That's the first point. Now, as Mr. Nice asked us to introduce the SFRY 1974 constitution here, I consider that we should not only have the 1974 constitution, which was not in force at the critical time we're discussing, but the latest constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as well, that is to say, before it was forcibly dismantled. So those are the two remarks I had to make, and now I want an explanation of a procedural nature. Mr. May, at the trial here on the 24th of April, 2002, took note of, and this is on page 3701 of the transcript, line 22, and I'm quoting what you said in that line: "It is the practice that additions to witness statements are accepted together with the statement itself." That is what you took note of yourself, and that is why I demand that the additions to the statement of this particular witness, the one who just left and which was disclosed by the Prosecution also be admitted into evidence as exhibits. And I have in mind the following additions: The addendum to the document that the Prosecutor disclosed as being an addition to the statement, Rugova, on the platform of the democratic alliance of Kosovo. The number of the document is, in the Serbian version, 03037052, and in the English version, it is K021410. Furthermore, it is -- this is also a document which was disclosed by Mr. Nice as an addition to the witness statement. It was entitled, "Rugova Cautions of the Radicalisation and Total War." The number of that document, the Serbian version, is 03036489 and K212002147.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please be asked to slow down when quoting figures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And also another document by Mr. Nice, Rugova speaking of a visit to Italy and the Pope. On the right-hand side --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness [sic] please quote the figures more slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're asked to quote figures slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last document, in the Serbian version, was 03037120, and the English version was -- I haven't got the English number, in fact, for that document. And finally, another document also produced by Mr. Nice, and it is 03036508 in the Serbian version, and in the English version it is K0214118. So on that same basis and on those same grounds that you explained yourself, I request that they be introduced along with the witness statement, according to standard practice as I was able to understand it from your own explanation, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With respect, no. The material was provided to him either under Rule 66 or Rule 68 for him to use for cross-examination if he wanted to. He sought to rely on one document for cross-examination, and since the exercise hadn't been conducted properly, I dealt with it for him in re-examination, and that interview then became relevant. The other documents are, I think - I haven't got them at hand - press releases or statements of one kind or another. They would need the witness's comments for them to become of any value to you. If they haven't been cross-examined on, they shouldn't now burden the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us see the documents. We have a balance here between an accused who is acting in person and of course the fact that documents should normally be put to the witness before they're exhibited, but it may be that we can find a way forward having in mind that this is a Bench of professional Judges. Could you give us the documents in due course, when you can find them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When we can find them. It won't be until later this afternoon or tomorrow morning. Yes, we'll do what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider the position then. May we have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon will take the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls Mr. Sejdi Lami.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this the witness who was going to give evidence the other day and did not get on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, it's not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's another one. Nonetheless, we should attempt to finish his evidence before the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Examined by Mr. Saxon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Sejdi Lami?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lami, were you born on the 8th of August, 1950?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born in the hamlet of Lama in the village of Vata in the municipality of Kacanik, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the hamlet of Lama in the village of Vata located about five to six kilometres north-west of the town of Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 14th of July, 2000, did you provide a statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor about the events that you witnessed and experienced in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 30th of January of this year, 2002, in the municipality of Kacanik in Kosovo, were you provided with a copy of the statement that you made in July of 2000 in the presence of representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and a presiding officer appointed by the Registrar of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to confirm that the copy of the statement provided to you was true and correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender the statement as an exhibit under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Prosecutor's Exhibit number 135.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Sejdi Lami is a 51-year-old male Kosovo Albanian Muslim from the hamlet of Lama in the village of Vata, in the municipality of Kacanik. He is married with three daughters who, in 1999, were aged between 4 and 7 years. Mr. Lami's statement describes the action of Serb forces in the village of Vata, in Kacanik, on the 13th of April, 1999. He will describe that there was no regular KLA presence in the village during the conflict. However, about a week prior to the attack by Serb forces, some 20 KLA soldiers stayed in a house in the witness's village. These KLA soldiers left the village the day before the attack on the village of Vata by Serb forces. The witness will describe how on the 13th of April, 1999, at about 5.00 in the morning, he saw four Pragas and six military trucks filled with about 100 VJ soldiers entering his village. The population realised that soldiers had also surrounded the nearby village of Slatina in the municipality of Kacanik and that others had arrived from the direction of Brod. At about a quarter to six in the morning, shooting began coming from the Pragas and from hand-held weapons. As a result, a large part of the population - about 300 people - began to walk towards the mountain -- the mountains, excuse me. There was constant shooting in their direction but nobody was hurt at that time. The witness and his family hid in a gorge by a stream and from there he was unable to observe the soldiers. Later on, however, he heard from others that four men from the village had been captured. The shooting stopped and the soldiers left the village at around 1600 hours. The witness and his brothers went along the gorge and found the bodies of four unarmed civilian men; Mahmut Caka, Hebib Lami, Rrahman Lami, and Brahim Lami, who had been captured by the VJ soldiers earlier that day. They brought the bodies to a house in the village and the same day, seven more bodies were brought to the village from different locations in the area. In the hamlets of Caka and Tifeku, most of the houses were burned. On the 14th and 15th of April, 1999, the entire population of the village fled. The witness and his family went to Macedonia. On the way to Macedonia, they were stopped by VJ soldiers who demanded money from them in order to let the people pass. The villagers paid 500 Deutschmarks to these soldiers. When Mr. Lami returned to his village on the 17th of July, 1999, he found his home looted of all of its valuables. The same fate had happened in other homes in the village. Of the 11 bodies that were initially buried in the village cemetery, the body of Ramadan Xhokli was reburied in the KLA cemetery because he had been an active KLA member at the time of his death. However, all the remaining victims were civilians. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement, you speak about the attack by Serb forces on your village and how the people left the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What date was that, precisely?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: On the 13th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct - and that's what we see from your statement - that up until that day, that is to say up until the 13th of April, you lived peacefully in the village. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Until 13th of April, we were living in fear. We were sheltering in the hills because of the Serb armed forces and the tanks. And they had -- they had burned all the houses in our village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did they burn the houses in your village? You say that you were attacked on the 13th of April.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: They had --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did they burn --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter apologises. The tanks had surrounded the houses in the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They surrounded the houses in the village on the 13trh and then they were burned. In Lama, only one house was burned. In Slatina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You're talking about an event that allegedly took place on the 13th of April, and what I'm asking you is this: Why did you send your women and children to Urosevac much earlier than that date? Because up until the 13th of April, according to your statement, nobody touched you.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: We withdrew our children from our villages. We sent them to Ferizaj because the Serb army kept shelling all the time. And whoever they captured, they maltreated them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you understood me. You said that you were shelled on the 13th of April. Now, why was it that you took them away before the 13th of April in view of the fact that nobody touched you up until the 13th of April and you yourself said you lived quietly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You asked him that. As I understood, his answer was this: They sent them away because the Serb army kept shelling, and that if anyone was captured, they were maltreated. That was his answer. That's before the 13th of April, he's saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But he says that the army shelled the place on the 13th of April, and I'm asking him why he sent them off in January or -- because between January and April, there's quite a lot of time. It's a long period.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I speak now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Answer this: Was there any shelling between January and the 13th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were shelling all over Kosova. Shelling went on to six, seven villages. The Serbs set houses on fire, committed crimes, killed people, injured people, and maltreated them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This was before the 13th of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, a moment ago you said that nothing happened before the 13th of April.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: I said nothing happened in my village. But from my village, Duraj, Gabrexh, Koxhaj, Dedaj villages, they were only three kilometres away from my house, they were all burned three, four days before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say that there were operations three or four days before the 13th of April, which means the 10th of April. And until the 13th, it didn't take place in your village, and up until the 10th, there was none in the surrounding areas either. My question to you is: Why, then, did you send the population off as early on as January when not even in the surrounding areas of your village before the 10th were there any operations going on?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: I want to tell you that I am speaking here about the 13th of April, about what I saw with my own eyes, what was perpetrated by the massacre that was perpetrated by the Serb army and the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I'm asking you why you sent them away, the women and children, in January to Urosevac when by the 10th, before the 10th, not even in the places around your village there were any clashes or conflicts of any kind.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: We sent our children away from the village because we felt that it was calmer in the city. On the 23rd of March, we brought the children from Ferizaj to the village because we heard that Ferizaj was going to be attacked by the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We're obviously not going to get anywhere with that question. But answer me my next question. Why, then, did you stay on in the village? You had sent your women and children off in January. Why did you yourself remain in the village?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: We stayed in the village after we sent away the children because for us it was easier to run and find refuge in the mountains, in gorges. But if you have small children -- some had children of two, three months, old or, five, six years old; it was hard for us to carry the children. That's why we sent them to Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men stayed on in the village?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Our village is not a big village. It has about 12 houses. We were two or three men. Just to look after the livestock and the cattle we had and the properties. But at that time, there was no KLA in our village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And how long were the soldiers of the KLA in your village?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: There was no KLA in my village, but nearby, about 200 or 300 metres away, in the place called Sopotnica, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were 200 or 300 metres away from your village and you said that they had put up in a house.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: That's right. In a house called the house of Emin Kastrati.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Well, there were -- there were 20, but half of them were in uniform and half them were in plainclothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: I didn't see weapons. I only know the house where they were, and I didn't see anything else. I didn't see them with any real weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did they stay there where you say they were, at a distance of 200 or 300 metres away from you?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: They stayed two or three days -- not two or three days. And then they went. And on the next day, Serbian forces attacked us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which unit of the KLA it was?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of this. I didn't take any interest in this sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps know what their commander's name was?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know those members of the KLA from before?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So none of them was from your village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: There were no members of the KLA from my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that they were digging trenches in your village?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: It is true. Above my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What? You say above your village? Did I get you right? Above your village. In the hill above your village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: That's right, above the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they need those trenches for?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: They dug them to defend the place and to defend the Albanian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them open fire from those positions of theirs, at the police and army?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: When the Serbian forces started, fortunately there was no KLA there, because then there would have been a worse massacre than at Racak because the population were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you know about Racak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a side issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he mentioned it. The witness mentioned the question of Racak. He said that it was worse than it was in Racak, so he knows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But what he knows isn't relevant. Move on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, can I tell you why it is relevant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said that it would have been worse than in Racak, because there were inhabitants here. The population was there. Which means that he knows that there was no -- there were no inhabitants in Racak, just the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to hear evidence about Racak in due course by people who were there. We'll hear evidence from them, not by somebody who was a long way away. Now let's get on with what he can deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that on the 24th of March, NATO started its bombing. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you claim that they bombed during the night only; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes. That's right and true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the intensity of the explosions that you heard during the night?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Explosion was great when the Serb forces shelled from a position in a village called Picrrak, where they were stationed. More than 200, 300 soldiers with tanks, armoured vehicles, everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But let's just see if we understand each other. You said that from the beginning of NATO's bombing, most of the farmers and their families had taken to the woods to hide in them because of the Serb shelling. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Because of the -- of the Serb bombing and shelling, we found shelter in the forest. But we were not at all afraid of the NATO bombing, because NATO didn't hit the civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, since you spent this time in the woods, you heard the explosions of NATO from the 24th onwards, what kind of shelling were you seeking shelter from in the woods when you say yourself that the shelling started only on the 13th of April? What kind of shelling were you seeking shelter from for all of 20 days? That is to say, from when the bombing of NATO started, from the 24th of March until the 13th of April.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: From the 24th of March, we were in the village, up to the 13th of April. From the 13th of April, when the offensive was launched on Cakaj, Lama, Sllatina villages, I don't know how many victims, casualties there were. We buried them on the 14th of April and then fled the village because we saw houses burned, people injured, and we were obliged to leave for Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please concentrate on the answer. You said that you were hiding in the woods all this time until the 13th of April. That is to say, from when the NATO bombing started. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: We hid in the mountains, in the forest, because of fear of Serb forces who entered the village and ransacked the houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said that the Serb forces entered on the 13th of April. I am asking you about the time up until the 13th of April. What were you hiding from between the 24th of March and the 13th of April?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: From the 24th of March to the 13th of April, we were hiding because of fear of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: We were afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did I understand you correctly then, the villagers did not leave the village because of the NATO bombing but were doing that because of Serb shelling; is that right? That is your assertion.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question? I am not so clear about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have understood from your explanation that the villagers did not leave the village because of NATO bombing but because they were afraid of Serb shelling. Was that your explanation?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we were afraid from the Serb army but not from NATO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you afraid of before the shelling which took place only on the 13th of April?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: But I said that we were afraid, and we hid out of fear of Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lami, was there any shelling from Serb forces before 13th of April, after the NATO bombing had started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was shelling in the mountains, in the surrounding areas, and in the village. In Pricrrak village, many houses were burned. In Biqefc village, many houses were burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So in your statement, page 2, the second paragraph, when you say, "NATO was bombing during the night and the Serbs shelled the village during the daytime," are you meaning -- did you mean the shelling of Serb forces which took place before the 13th of April offensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I mean before the 13th of April when they shelled other villages. This is why we were afraid and took shelter in the mountains and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. At the outset, you said that this previous shelling, before the 13th, could have been three or four days prior to that. That is to say, on the 10th of April at the earliest. And you were hiding in the hills all the time, ever since the bombing started. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We -- we were found in between the villages that were being shelled. And so we were afraid and had to leave. On the 13th of April, they attacked our village. At 5.00 in the morning, the Serb army blocked three or four neighbourhoods of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But just a short while ago, the soldiers of the KLA, as you call them, you say they were 200 metres away from you, all the way up to the day on the eve of the 13th, you said that they ran away on a particular day, and the next day, the shelling started. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They left one day before we were attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were you hiding then until that day when they left when they were present there all the time? Wasn't their protection sufficient for you? Why did you flee into the forests 20 days before, when the NATO aggression started?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: I have no idea why they left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that your family, approximately one week before what you call the Serb attack on your village, tried to go to Macedonia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you decide to do that when the KLA was there right by you, 200 metres away, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: My family left after the KLA left the village, after the offensive. And during that offensive, I said there was no KLA present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Lami. Let us try to get the timing right. Today, just a little while ago, you said that the KLA left the village one day before the offensive started; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: The KLA didn't know that there would be an offensive against our village, but I have no idea why the KLA left. And they were not regular forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was not why they left. That doesn't matter. It's quite clear why they ran away. But the question was whether this was, in terms of time, one day before the attack. That's what you had said. Is that right or not? They left one day prior to the attack. That was your assertion.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
